```{r setup}
library(treeshapesim)
set.seed(1)
```

## Two shape statistics, two processes

The gamma statistic of Pybus and Harvey (2000) summarizes the distribution of
branching times: it is near zero for Yule trees and negative when branching
times are concentrated near the root. The Colless index summarizes topological
imbalance; normalized against its Yule expectation, it is near zero for Yule
trees and positive for more imbalanced ones. `tree_shape()` returns both.

`sim_tree_shape()` draws the topology from Aldous' beta-splitting model
(`beta`) and the internode intervals from a pure-birth process in which each of
the k lineages splits at rate k^c (`c`). The two are drawn independently, gamma
depends only on the intervals and the Colless index only on the topology, so
`c` moves gamma without changing the Colless index and `beta` does the
opposite.

```{r}
yule <- sim_tree_shape(100, nsim = 50)
early <- sim_tree_shape(100, c = -1, nsim = 50)
imbalanced <- sim_tree_shape(100, beta = -1.5, nsim = 50)
shapes <- lapply(list(yule = yule, early = early, imbalanced = imbalanced),
                 function(trees) colMeans(t(vapply(trees, tree_shape, numeric(2)))))
do.call(rbind, shapes)
```

## Reaching target values

The mean of each statistic depends on its parameter and on the number of tips.
`calibrate_shape()` estimates both curves for a given number of tips, and
`shape_params()` inverts them. Since each curve is estimated from its own
process, without building trees, the calibration is fast. Use more draws per
value (`reps`, 200 by default) for a study; a few are enough here.

```{r}
cal <- calibrate_shape(100, reps = 50)
cal
shape_params(cal, gamma = -2, colless = 1)
```

The parameters give the target values on average, but single trees vary around
them. `sim_tree_target()` keeps only trees whose statistics fall within a
tolerance of the targets. Because topology and intervals are independent, it
rejects them separately, which gives the same distribution of trees as
rejecting whole trees, with a much higher acceptance rate.

```{r}
trees <- sim_tree_target(100, gamma = -2, colless = 1, nsim = 20, tol = 0.25,
                         calibration = cal, root_age = 50)
summary(attr(trees, "shape"))
attr(trees, "acceptance")
```

## A grid of tree shapes

For simulation studies, `shape_grid()` crosses levels of both statistics. The
levels can come, for instance, from quantiles of `tree_shape()` over empirical
trees of a similar size; here they are set by hand.

```{r}
grid <- shape_grid(100, gamma = c(-2, -1, 0), colless = c(0, 0.5, 1),
                   calibration = cal)
grid
cell <- grid[grid$gamma == -1 & grid$colless == 0.5, ]
cell_trees <- sim_tree_target(100, gamma = cell$gamma, colless = cell$colless,
                              nsim = 10, calibration = cal)
```

## Placing an empirical tree on the same scale

`fit_shape()` estimates `beta` from the topology and `c` from the branching
times by maximum likelihood (the beta-splitting model and the DDX model of the
R package laser, with `c = -x`), and a parametric bootstrap with the package's
own generators gives percentile intervals. The estimate of `beta` is imprecise
for balanced trees with few tips, and `c` describes the shape of the
lineage-through-time curve, not its cause.

```{r}
empirical <- sim_tree_shape(150, beta = -1, c = -0.7)   # stands in for a real tree
fit_shape(empirical, boot = 30)
```

incomplete molecular phylogenies. *Proceedings of the Royal Society B*, 267,
2267–2272. https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2000.1278
